name: Marri Tjevin
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Mansfield, John & Ian Green. 2021. Fricative contrasts and neutralization in Marri Tjevin. Australian Journal of Linguistics 41(2): 220-261. doi:10.1080/07268602.2021.1957774. Read from the open author accepted manuscript (49 pp., Minerva Access hdl 11343/297846)
catalog_locator: AM pagination: sec.3 p.5; sec.5 p.21; sec.5.1 pp.21-24 (Figs 8-12, fn.12 on p.23, tonic-syllable definition p.24); sec.5.3 ex.(35) (simple verb pi 'do, say'). Journal pages 220-261 not mapped.
catalog_quote: [sec.3, AM p.5] We have not observed contrastive stress in Marri Tjevin, nor have we observed canonical lexical stress effects in terms of vowel duration and vowel quality (cf. Mansfield, forthcoming). However, the accentual alignment system does reflect word structure ... [sec.5, p.21] Although there has not been any detailed research on Marri Tjevin prosody, we here describe the fundamentals of pitch accent positioning, which is the clearest observed form of prosodic prominence. Pitch accents occur at the beginning of the word in simple words such as nouns, but in complex verbs the pitch accent is instead anchored to the word-medial coverb. [sec.5.1, pp.21-23] In simple words, pitch accent occurs near the beginning of the word. ... The classifier proclitics shown here are not prosodically prominent and do not alter accentual alignment on the following noun ... In these complex verbs, the pitch accent is not anchored to the beginning of the word, but rather to the coverb. If the coverb is disyllabic, then the pitch accent aligns on its first syllable (Figure 11). But if the coverb is monosyllabic, the pitch accent usually instead aligns on the preceding syllable (Figures 12). [p.24] We label the syllable to which pitch accents are anchored as the ‘tonic syllable’. The tonic is therefore the first syllable of simple words, the first syllable of a disyllabic coverb in complex verbs, or the syllable preceding a monosyllabic coverb.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word prominence in Marri Tjevin is a pitch accent whose position is predictable from word structure: in simple words (nouns etc.) it is anchored to the first syllable of the word (classifier proclitics such as a=, ða= are not prominent and do not shift it); in complex (coverb) verbs it is anchored to the coverb - on the first syllable of a disyllabic coverb, or on the syllable immediately preceding a monosyllabic coverb. Stress is not contrastive and shows no duration/vowel-quality correlates.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated for Marri Tjevin (only one pitch accent per word is described). Mansfield 2022 sec.5.4 reports second-hand that other Western Daly languages have initial primary stress with secondary stress on the coverb-initial syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Complex verbs: accent on the coverb rather than word-initially; monosyllabic coverbs: accent on the preceding syllable; fn.12: 'some apparent variation in accentual alignment in complex verbs'; simple (coverb-less) inflected verbs pattern like simple words with accent near the beginning. Pitch peak often realised late (boundary of syllables 1-2), interpreted as a phonetic 'late rise'. Authors caution that Marri Tjevin prosody has not been researched in detail.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level prominence (pitch accent per phonological word incl. proclitic classifiers, which are extrametrical); evidence from elicited words/sentences and narrative in field recordings (Wadeye 2012-2017, two fluent elders) plus 1990s and 1986 archival recordings. Authors explicitly deny contrastive/lexical stress; the reading 'fixed: initial syllable' applies to simple words, with morphologically anchored (coverb) prominence in complex verbs - a catalog entry should carry that caveat (alternative coding: morphologically determined).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes 'Marri Tjevin' (= Maridjabin/Marityabin/Marritjevin/Marrisjabin, ISO zmj, mari1421), language of the Rak Thangkurral and Rak Nadirri, recorded at Wadeye 2012-2017 from two elders plus Green's 1990s and Kofod's 1986 recordings. The authors treat Marri Tjevin and Marri Amu (Marriammu, ISO xru) as 'largely a shared linguistic code' and drew on sources labelled both; Tryon 1974:101 likewise calls their phonologies identical. Glottolog places mari1421 under Western Daly > Bringen > Marithielic together with Marrithiyel, Marri Ammu, Marri Dan (the 'Brinkin dialect cluster'). Green 1989's stem-initial stress rule is for the sister dialect Marrithiyel, not Marri Tjevin.

sources.note: Sec.3 (AM p.5): no contrastive stress observed, no canonical lexical stress effects (vowel duration/quality), but 'the accentual alignment system does reflect word structure'. Sec.5/5.1 (AM pp.21-24): pitch accent anchored to the beginning of the word (tonic = first syllable) in simple words such as nouns, classifier proclitics not prominent; in complex verbs the accent is anchored to the coverb (first syllable of a disyllabic coverb, or the syllable preceding a monosyllabic coverb); fn.12 some variation, prosody not researched in detail. sources.citation: Green, Ian. 1989. Marrithiyel: a language of the Daly River region of Australia's Northern Territory. PhD thesis, Australian National University.
sources.note: Sec.1.4: Marrisjabin, Marri Ammu and Marridan are named by Marrithiyel speakers as dialects of 'one language'; Green did no fieldwork on them and reports no phonological differences known for the western dialects. Sec.2.1.3 Word Stress (pp.33-36) describes MARRITHIYEL only: primary stress on the first syllable of a stem, secondary on the second syllable thereafter; class prefixes do not shift stress. Sister dialect, not Marri Tjevin data.
